claims.text: Controlled annealing between 600 and 1100 °C reversibly modifies dislocation core structures in HfNbTaTiZr.
Controlled annealing between 600 and 1100 °C enhances chemical short-range ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Dislocation-core modifications and chemical short-range ordering cause changes in the stress–strain response of HfNbTaTiZr.
Dislocation-core modifications and chemical short-range ordering cause changes in the thermal expansion of HfNbTaTiZr.
Dislocation-core modifications and chemical short-range ordering cause changes in the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr.
Plastic deformation in the relevant elevated-temperature regime is dislocation-mediated and thermally activated.
Increasing temperature from the lower to the upper part of the 600–1100 °C range changes the dominant carrier of plasticity from screw dislocations to edge dislocations.
The baseline alloy is an as-processed, homogenized HfNbTaTiZr alloy with an equiaxed microstructure.
Annealed samples will have lower flow stress than the untreated baseline between 600 and 1100 °C.
Annealed samples will exhibit stabilized or increased elastic modulus relative to the untreated baseline.
Annealed samples will have lower thermal expansion coefficients than the untreated baseline between 600 and 1100 °C.
A distinct deformation-mechanism transition may occur near the middle of the 600–1100 °C interval.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply throughout 600–1100 °C.
Outside 600–1100 °C, other thermally activated phenomena or phase transformations may dominate.
In situ neutron diffraction can be used to obtain elastic moduli, with resonant ultrasound spectroscopy providing a complementary determination.
The quantitative shifts in flow stress, elastic modulus, and thermal expansion coefficient are uncertain.
The effects of dislocation-core modification and chemical ordering may overlap and be difficult to separate experimentally.
